title: The `–refresh-times` option doesn’t seem to work for an encrypted onedrive remote

#### The associated forum post URL from `https://<redacted-host>`
https://<redacted-host>/t/the-refresh-times-option-doesnt-seem-to-work-for-an-encrypted-onedrive-remote/47888/1


#### What is the problem you are having with rclone?
The `--refresh-times` option doesn't seem to work for my encrypted onedrive remote.

This is a follow on from my [bug report](https://<redacted-host>/t/after-upgrade-rclone-sync-wants-to-do-a-full-copy-not-just-of-deltas/47864/8) and subsequent issue #8090.  I reopened the issue but it didn't get visibility

If I sync a single file and then an lsl of the remote file, I can see that it still only has one-second resolution, not millisecond resolution. A subsequent run of sync still reports that it has to adjust the modification time. That is, it appears `--refresh-times` is not working.


#### What is your rclone version (output from `rclone version`)
```
rclone v1.68.0
- os/version: ubuntu 22.04 (64 bit)
- os/kernel: 5.15.0-101-generic (x86_64)
- os/type: linux
- os/arch: amd64
- go/version: go1.23.1
- go/linking: static
- go/tags: none
```


#### Which OS you are using and how many bits (e.g. Windows 7, 64 bit)
Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS


#### Which cloud storage system are you using? (e.g. Google Drive)
Encrypted OneDrive


#### The command you were trying to run (e.g. `rclone copy /tmp remote:tmp`)
```
rclone -vv sync --refresh-times ~/repos/photos/data/1/1202 onedrive:repos/photos/data/1
```
Then
```
rclone lsl ~/repos/photos/data/1/1202
rclone lsl onedrive:repos/photos/data/1/1202
```

#### A log from the command with the `-vv` flag (e.g. output from `rclone -vv copy /tmp remote:tmp`)

The key part appears to be that the mtime of the onedrive file still only has precision to a whole second.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
What kind of onedrive are you using?

Can you include the output of `rclone config redacted` please?

I did a test and I'm satisfied that `--refresh-times` is working properly on a onedrive personal wrapped with crypt.

Edited highlights

```
$ rclone sync -vv /tmp/src 'secret,remote="onedrive:secrets":'
$ touch /tmp/src/dir/file.txt
$ rclone sync -vv /tmp/src --refresh-times 'secret,remote="onedrive:secrets":'
INFO  : dir/file.txt: Updated modification time in destination
$ rclone sync -vv /tmp/src 'secret,remote="onedrive:secrets":'
DEBUG : dir/file.txt: Size and modification time the same (differ by -373.028µs, within tolerance 1ms)
DEBUG : dir/file.txt: Unchanged skipping
```

> If I sync a single file and then an lsl of the remote file, I can see that it still only has one-second resolution, not millisecond resolution.

So you uploaded a file but it only has 1 second resolution? And then the resolution did not change when we changed it.

What kind of file is this?

Does it do this for all files? Or just this type of file?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> So you uploaded a file but it only has 1 second resolution? And then the resolution did not change when we changed it.
> What kind of file is this?
> Does it do this for all files? Or just this type of file?

The files are the contents of a borgbackup repository - git-ish incremental backups.  In this context, they are just standard files.  Normally I just do a vanilla `sync`, but this was before doing an upgrade to the latest `rclone`.

Once I upgraded, the large sync was taking too long, and so I investigated.  This mtime mismatch was happening on all the files, forcing a full upload.

To troubleshoot, I devolved the problem into the simplest replicable (for me) use case - that of syncing a single file.  That's what this issue reports against.  For this single file use case, the `--refresh-times` flag doesn't actually seem to refresh the times.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: Maybe the difference between your test above and mine is that in mine the files already exist with whole-second precision on the timestamp (created by a pre-1.66 version), whereas yours is going to get the timestamp from the file as it puts it

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> Maybe the difference between your test above and mine is that in mine the files already exist with whole-second precision on the timestamp (created by a pre-1.66 version), whereas yours is going to get the timestamp from the file as it puts it

That worked for me - here the upload was made with v1.65.2 and you can see v1.68.1 correcting the times with `--refresh-times`

```
$ rclone-v1.65.2 sync -vv /tmp/src 'secret,remote="onedrive:secrets":'
$ rclone lsl 'secret,remote="onedrive:secrets":'
        6 2024-09-25 15:14:39.000000000 dir/file.txt
  3538536 2024-09-25 12:23:49.000000000 dir/test.jpg
$ rclone-v1.68.1 sync -vv /tmp/src --refresh-times 'secret,remote="onedrive:secrets":'
INFO  : dir/file.txt: Updated modification time in destination
INFO  : dir/test.jpg: Updated modification time in destination
$ rclone lsl 'secret,remote="onedrive:secrets":'
        6 2024-09-25 15:14:39.268000000 dir/file.txt
  3538536 2024-09-25 12:23:49.422000000 dir/test.jpg
```

I wonder whether these old files are different somehow and can't take a ms precision timestamp, but only a 1s timestamp precision.

You could see if new files can take ms precision. Can you try uploading a new file and try the `--refresh-times` on a sync after `touch`-ing the local one?

comments.body:
OK, on _one_ of my remotes this is happening again and again, so I'm able to get a debug log.

```
2024/09/25 16:33:57 DEBUG : rclone: Version "v1.68.0" starting with parameters ["/home/<user>/bin/rclone" "--config" "/home/<user>/.config/rclone/rclone.conf" "--delete-before" "--rc" "--log-level" "DEBUG" "--log-file" "/BACKUP/NO_SYNC/log/20240925_OneDriveBackups3:.txt" "--stats=60s" "sync" "." "OneDriveBackups3:" "--include" "brains/**" "--include" "monitor/**" "--include" "openwrt/**" "--include" "pugwash/**" "--include" "switches/**" "--include" "tplink-a7/**" "--include" "monitor9/**" "--include" "hass9/**" "--include" "plexserver9/**" "--include" "phoenix/**"]
```

It starts off good...

```
2024/09/25 16:34:02 DEBUG : switches/20200720-basement-switch.cfg: Size and modification time the same (differ by 0s, within tolerance 1ms)
2024/09/25 16:34:02 DEBUG : switches/20200720-basement-switch.cfg: Unchanged skipping
2024/09/25 16:34:02 DEBUG : switches/20200720-living-switch.cfg: Size and modification time the same (differ by 0s, within tolerance 1ms)
```

But then a little later...

```
2024/09/25 16:34:03 DEBUG : brains/20240829._boot.4.gz_aa: Modification times differ by -909.387934ms: 2024-08-29 00:15:45.909387934 -0400 EDT, 2024-08-29 04:15:45 +0000 UTC
2024/09/25 16:34:03 DEBUG : brains/20240829.log: Modification times differ by -68.388101ms: 2024-08-29 00:15:46.068388101 -0400 EDT, 2024-08-29 04:15:46 +0000 UTC
2024/09/25 16:34:03 DEBUG : brains/20240829.root.4.gz_aa: Modification times differ by -257.383046ms: 2024-08-29 00:15:41.257383046 -0400 EDT, 2024-08-29 04:15:41 +0000 UTC
```

Let's look at the last of these:

```
% stat /BACKUP/brains/20240829.root.4.gz_aa                      
  File: /BACKUP/brains/20240829.root.4.gz_aa
  Size: 140938358       Blocks: 275552     IO Block: 4096   regular file
Device: fd05h/64773d    Inode: 81166355    Links: 1
Access: (0660/-rw-rw----)  Uid: (    0/    root)   Gid: (    0/    root)
Access: 2024-09-25 14:19:52.965512601 -0400
Modify: 2024-08-29 00:15:41.257383046 -0400
Change: 2024-08-29 00:15:42.569384424 -0400
 Birth: 2024-08-29 00:15:06.024346027 -0400
```

This is looking like OneDrive is only doing 1 second accuracy, and _not_ millisecond.

(Why didn't that show on the switch files?  Huh stat shows .0000 as the last modified time; I guess that must have originally been written on a filesystem without ms accuracy and just copied over!)

What's odd is that the other backups (OneDriveBackup1:  and OneDriveBackup2:) don't show this!

The 3 crypt's are set up the same
```
OneDriveBackups]
type = crypt
remote = OneDriveSweharris2:Backups
filename_encryption = off
directory_name_encryption = false
password = XXX
password2 = XXX

[OneDriveBackups2]
type = crypt
remote = OneDriveSweharris3:Backups
filename_encryption = off
directory_name_encryption = false
password = XXX
password2 = XXX

[OneDriveBackups3]
type = crypt
remote = OneDriveSweharris:Onedrive Only/BACKUP3
filename_encryption = off
directory_name_encryption = false
password = XXX
password2 = XXX
```

The underlying remotes are similar:

```
[OneDriveSweharris]
type = onedrive
token = ...
drive_id = ...
drive_type = personal

[OneDriveSweharris2]
type = onedrive
token = ...
drive_id = ...
drive_type = personal

[OneDriveSweharris3]
type = onedrive
token = ...
drive_id = ...
drive_type = personal
```

The only difference _might_ be in the creation of the OneDrive itself.  OneDriveSweharris1 was my original "created with outlook" drive.  I then converted that to a family plan.  "2" and "3" were created with the family plan.  This _shouldn't_ make a difference, but it's the only one I can see!

Now looking at a new file uploaded today using `rclone lsl ...`

```
% rclone lsl OneDriveBackups3:brains | grep 20240925
     1052 2024-09-25 00:15:23.000000000 20240925._boot.3.gz_aa
     2800 2024-09-25 00:15:23.000000000 20240925.log
 61238918 2024-09-25 00:15:21.000000000 20240925.root.3.gz_aa
```

So this brand new file still only has one second accuracy!

But on another remote:

```
% rclone lsl OneDriveBackups:penfold | grep 20240925.log
     7028 2024-09-25 01:06:55.174000000 20240925.log
```
We can see it got milliseconds.

Looking at the original `GET /v1.0/drives/XXX/root` call I also see some differences.

penfold (1ms) has a cTag in the JSON, brains doesn't.

webURL for brains (1s) also has an `id` field:

brains: `"webUrl": "https://<redacted-host>?cid=XXX&id=YYY",`
penfold: `"webUrl": "https://<redacted-host>/?cid=XXX",`

penfold has additional data in the JSON

```
  "createdBy": {
    "application": {
      "displayName": "OneDrive website",
      "id": "44048800"
    },
```

eTag on brains: `  "eTag": "\"{GUID},139\"",`
on penfold: `  "eTag": "XXX",`

In all cases (both the "root" and the file above), all timestamps for penfold have SS.uuuZ microseconds, but brains is just SSZ second accuracy.
eg
`  "lastModifiedDateTime": "2024-09-25T20:33:55.187Z",`
vs
`  "lastModifiedDateTime": "2024-09-25T21:15:11Z",`

> (Interestingly, but not relevent to this problem, brains has quickXorHash, penfold has quickXorHash _and_ sha1Hash _and_ sha256Hash).
> 
> These look like two totally different backends!!

That is interesting info. penfold (1ms) having those hashes means it is based off the onedrive personal line. Whereas brains (1s) looks like it is based off onedrive business which never had sha1 or sha256. However Microsoft have deprecated the sha1 and sha256 hashes so migrating to a platform that doesn't have them makes sense. My guess is that they are trying to merge the OneDrive Personal and Business infrastructure.

I've noticed before that Microsoft's infrastructure (not surprisingly for something so big) is not homogeneous.

So if Microsoft are migrating OneDrive accounts to backends which only support 1s time resolution then we should probably revert the 1ms change.

I don't think that 1ms time accuracy is documented anywhere.

@participant3 did you find documentation for it somewhere? The API docs I've see are all a bit vague about what a timestamp is.

If we do revert the 1 ms precision can anyone think of any negative consequences. What about bisync?

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: For testing purposes I added `--modify-window 1s` to my calls, and it worked as expected for my `sync` calls.  I don't use `bisync` but I can't think it'd break anything; anything that was more than 1ms different would already trigger a copy and I can't imagine someone changing a file 10 times a second and expecting each copy to get sync'd; it takes longer than that to copy the file!

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
> @participant3 did you find documentation for it somewhere? The API docs I've see are all a bit vague about what a timestamp is.

I agree that the docs are vague, and I would also call them inconsistent. For instance, [this example](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/driveitem-list-versions?view=graph-rest-1.0&tabs=http#response-1) shows a `lastModifiedDateTime` with 3 decimal places (`2017-09-14T12:34:53.912Z`), while [this one](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/driveitem-get?view=graph-rest-1.0&tabs=http#response-1) shows no decimal.

> If we do revert the 1 ms precision can anyone think of any negative consequences. What about bisync?

Bisync should be fine -- in theory it should be the same as just manually overriding the precision with `--modify-window 1s`. There's a theoretical risk that two files could be considered equal when they are not, but in practice I think the risk would be very small, as the files would have to have an identical size and modtimes that differ by a fraction of a second.

One thing I wonder is what happens to a file that's already on onedrive with a more precise modtime before this migration. Does the existing decimal data disappear in the API response? Or does it only affect files created/updated after the migration? The former could possibly cause surprises if people are (for example) scripting with the output of `lsl`, or something.
